the differences in evolutionary trends and rates between the rodent and human malaria lineages are due to differences in the host lineages themselves, and not due to the parasite lineages.

the differences observed in patterns of molecular evolution among these lineages reflect both differences in the selective pressures acting on the parasites and differences in the effective sizes of the host lineages, which may be related to differences in their population structures.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evolution of the Plasmodium genome is shaped by the host-parasite interaction, with host-driven selection being a key factor in determining patterns and rates of molecular evolution.
the parasite genomes infecting the human lineage have evolved faster than those infecting the murid lineages.

the parasite genomes that have coevolved with the human lineage are less constrained, and thus more susceptible to the accumulation of deleterious mutations, than the genomes that have co-evolved with murine hosts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
host adaptation is a critical driver of the evolution of malaria parasites and that this adaptation is likely highly dependent on the host species.

the parasite genomes infecting humans have been evolving at faster rates than those of their rodent counterparts and that this may be due to a lower effective size of hominid parasites and relaxed selective constraints on their genes.

, while host-parasite interaction genes evolve rapidly, the host lineage itself has a major impact on the evolution of the parasite genome, with the hominid and rodent lineages evolving at different rates and under different selective pressures.
